questions.q: State the definition of molar specific heat capacity and its SI unit.
questions.a: Molar specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by one kelvin. Its SI unit is \(\text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). A wrong answer (e.g., giving \(\text{J kg}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\)) reveals confusion between specific heat capacity (per unit mass) and molar specific heat capacity (per unit amount of substance).

questions.q: Why do gases have two molar specific heat capacities (\(C_p\) and \(C_v\)) while solids and liquids are usually described by only one?
questions.a: Gases expand significantly when heated at constant pressure, doing work on the surroundings; thus extra heat is needed compared to constant volume where no work is done. Solids and liquids expand negligibly, so the work done is extremely small and \(C_p \approx C_v\). A wrong answer ignoring the work done during expansion indicates a lack of understanding of the first law of thermodynamics (\( \Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W \)) applied to thermal processes.

questions.q: The specific heat capacity of nitrogen gas (\(N_2\)) is \(1040 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). Its molar mass is \(28 \text{ g mol}^{-1}\). Calculate the molar specific heat capacity of nitrogen at constant volume. (Assume the given specific heat is \(c_v\)).
questions.a:
Given: \(c_v = 1040 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\), \(M = 28 \text{ g mol}^{-1} = 0.028 \text{ kg mol}^{-1}\).
Formula: \(C_v = c_v \times M\).
Substitution: \(C_v = 1040 \times 0.028 = 29.12 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\).
Unit check: \(\text{J kg}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \times \text{kg mol}^{-1} = \text{J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\).
A wrong answer of \(29120 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\) reveals the student used molar mass in grams without converting to kilograms, a critical unit conversion error.

questions.q: For an ideal diatomic gas, \(C_v = 20.8 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\) and \(C_p = 29.1 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). If the gas is heated at constant pressure, what fraction of the supplied heat energy goes into increasing the internal energy of the gas?
questions.a:
At constant pressure, \(\Delta Q = n C_p \Delta T\). The increase in internal energy is \(\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T\) (since internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature).
Fraction = \(\frac{\Delta U}{\Delta Q} = \frac{C_v}{C_p} = \frac{20.8}{29.1} \approx 0.715\) (or 71.5%).
A wrong answer using \(C_p/C_v\) or \(1 - C_v/C_p\) reveals confusion about the energy partition between internal energy and work done during expansion.

questions.q: A student solves a problem: "2 moles of oxygen gas are heated at constant volume from 300 K to 350 K. Heat supplied = 5000 J. Find \(C_v\)." The student writes: \(C_v = \frac{Q}{n \Delta T} = \frac{5000}{2 \times 50} = 50 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\). Evaluate this solution.
questions.a: The calculation is mathematically correct, but the result \(50 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\) is physically unreasonable for oxygen gas (typical \(C_v \approx 21 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\)). The error is likely in the problem data (heat supplied too high) or the student misread "constant pressure" as "constant volume" (where \(C_p \approx 29 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}\)). A student who only checks arithmetic misses the physical plausibility check.

questions.q: Design a simple school-lab experiment to determine the molar specific heat capacity at constant pressure (\(C_p\)) of air using a constant-pressure gas thermometer setup (e.g., a flask with a volume-adjustable syringe). Outline the measurements needed and the calculation steps.
questions.a: Apparatus: Conical flask with a movable piston/syringe (constant pressure), heater, thermometer, balance. Procedure: (1) Measure mass of air in flask (by mass difference after flushing). (2) Convert mass to moles using molar mass of air (~29 g/mol). (3) Supply known heat \(Q\) (electrical: \(VIt\)). (4) Measure temperature rise \(\Delta T\) at constant pressure (piston moves freely). (5) Calculate \(C_p = Q / (n \Delta T)\). A poor answer omits the constant-pressure condition (fixed piston) or forgets to convert mass to moles.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Molar specific heat capacity is the amount of heat energy required to raise the ______ of one mole of a substance by one kelvin (or one degree Celsius).
Fill in the blank: Observe a domestic LPG cylinder: we purchase gas by mass (kg), but chemists and physicists often quantify it in moles for ______ calculations.
What is Molar specific heat capacity? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Molar specific heat capacity is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by one kelvin (or one degree Celsius).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Molar specific heat capacity?
questions.a: Students treat molar specific heat capacity as numerically equal to specific heat capacity, ignoring the molar mass conversion factor.
